parts.text:
You read part of an interview. An analyst asked one future user of a software service a series of questions. You decide, for each question, whether it follows up the answer given just before it.

A question follows up the previous answer when it asks about something that answer said: it asks the speaker to explain, give an example of, say more about, or say why of something the answer mentioned, or it picks up a particular thing the answer named. Wording does not matter; a question can follow up an answer without repeating any of its words.

A question does not follow up the previous answer when it turns to something that answer did not mention, even if the speaker said it in an earlier answer, even if it stays with the same broad subject, and even if it is a good question. A general question that could follow any answer, such as whether there is anything else, does not follow up either.

You receive the pairs of the interview after its first question: for each later question, the answer given just before it, and the question.

Reply with JSON only: an object with one key, "questions", a list with exactly one entry for every pair, in the same order. Each entry has "id", the question's id, and "follow_up", true or false.

Q2
The answer just before it: I plan and run flights for my company, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight. Several of us plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves.
The question: What do you need to know about a drone before you choose it for a flight, and what should stop you from choosing it?

Q3
The answer just before it: I need to know which model it is, how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses. My company's policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight.
The question: When several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same drone or site, what goes wrong, and what should the service do about it?

Q4
The answer just before it: Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and the same popular drones. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. I know nothing about software, so I cannot say what the service should do about it.
The question: Is it ever acceptable for one drone to be planned for two flights whose times overlap, or for a site to have more drones taking off or landing at once than it has places for?

Q5
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: If two dispatchers both plan the same drone for the same time, what happens in real life when the time comes?

Q6
The answer just before it: I don't know.
The question: What does "signing off" a flight involve: what do you check or confirm before you sign, and can anything change in the plan after you have signed?

Q7
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. A dispatcher can call off a flight. I know nothing about software, so I cannot say what the service does or what checks are involved in signing off.
The question: Who else, besides dispatchers, can make a flight leave, change it or call it off?

Q8
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and a dispatcher can call off a flight. I don't know who else can make a flight leave, change it, or call it off.
The question: Is a flight one trip from a takeoff site to a destination, or can it have several stops, and what information does a flight plan contain?

Q9
The answer just before it: Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, while inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. Drones fly along corridors between named sites. I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves.
The question: Where do jobs come from: who creates a delivery or inspection job, and what does a job say (load weight, deadlines, points, sensors needed)?

Q10
The answer just before it: I don't know who creates a delivery or inspection job. Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started.
The question: Before you sign off a flight, what must be true about the drone, the load, the battery range and the way it flies for the flight to be safe and allowed?

Q11
The answer just before it: I decide which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. Deliveries carry a load from one site to another, and inspections take a drone with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order and bring it back to where the inspection started. I don't know what else must be true about the drone, the load, the battery range, or the way it flies.
The question: When an airspace closure affects a flight you planned or one that is already in the air, what do you need to be told, and what do you then do?

Q12
The answer just before it: The authorities announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once, and these closures are often amended during the day. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. I can call off a flight, but I don't know what else I am told or what I then do.
The question: Should the service refuse to let you sign off a flight whose way goes through a corridor that is closed by the authorities at the time of the flight, or only warn you?

Q13
The answer just before it: I know nothing about software, so I cannot say what the service should do or how it should handle a flight whose way goes through a closed corridor. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce closures. A closure can come into force while drones are already in the air, and I am a dispatcher who can call off a flight.
The question: When a technician has taken a drone out of service for repairs, do you ever fly it?

Q14
The answer just before it: I don't know whether a drone taken out of service for repairs is ever flown. I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies and sign off a flight before it leaves.
The question: Does your company ever share a site, a drone, or a corridor with another drone company, for example at a hospital or a common hub?

Q15
The answer just before it: Each company has its own charging pads at its own sites, and pads are never lent to another company. A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and customers accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone. I don't know whether my company shares a site, a drone, or a corridor with another company.
The question: After a flight, what do you or your company need to keep or look back on, and for how long?

Q16
The answer just before it: I don't know what we need to keep or look back on, or for how long. None of the companies is seeking certification from the platform, and we expect it to respect how the rules work in practice.
The question: If a regulator asks about a flight, must your company be able to show which dispatcher signed it off and when?

Q17
The answer just before it: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I don't know whether my company must be able to show a regulator which dispatcher signed it off and when. None of the companies is seeking certification from the platform, and we expect it to respect how the rules work in practice.
The question: While a flight is in the air, do you follow where the drone is, and how do you know when it has arrived or come back?

Q18
The answer just before it: Nobody watches every drone at every moment, and one person may be responsible for hundreds. Radio coverage is patchy, and reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. People and devices outside the company report when the drone arrives.
The question: Who are the people and devices outside the company that report a drone's arrival, and what are they allowed to see or do?

Q19
The answer just before it: I don't know who the people and devices outside the company are, or what they are allowed to see or do. People and devices outside the company report whether the load is ready, whether the drone reaches the points of its job, and whether the drone arrives.
The question: Since you are responsible for hundreds of drones, which situations during a flight must be brought to your attention?

Q20
The answer just before it: Nobody watches every drone at every moment, and one person may be responsible for hundreds. Radio coverage is patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather. I don't know which specific situations during a flight must be brought to my attention.
The question: If nobody has reported that the load is ready, may a delivery flight still leave?
